Douglas Adams. The British author and humorist whose The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy defined comedic science fiction for generations. Blending absurdist humor with genuine philosophical speculation, Adams interrogated meaning, existence, and bureaucracy across galaxies with the same anxious wit he brought to terrestrial social critique. He elevated the comic premise to philosophical vehicle, making profound questions feel inevitable consequences of the ridiculous. The Hitchhiker's Guide, published in 1979, follows the accidental space traveler Arthur Dent through an absurdist cosmos ruled by improbable bureaucracy and alien incompetence. Within its pages, Adams created the Deep Thought supercomputer, which calculates the Answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything as 42—a joke about the impossibility of existential certainty. Beyond this massive work, he authored the Dirk Gently detective series, applying the same comedic speculation to contemporary England, tracking how the Holistic Detective navigates impossible causalities. Adams's style deployed rapid-fire absurdist humor, portmanteau wordplay, and deflationary punchlines, descending from radio comedy rather than literary tradition. His speculative premises exist primarily to create incongruity and philosophical vertigo—the mismatch between human expectation and cosmic reality. He merged profound pessimism about meaning with exuberant formal play, suggesting that laughter is the only sane response to existence.
